nodes.label: Bryan D. Palmer
nodes.date_label: ‘Most Uncommon Common Men’ 1976 · A Culture in Conflict 1979 · ‘Response to Joan Scott’ 1987 · Descent into Discourse 1990 · E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions 1994 · ‘Radical Reasoning’ 2009
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of labour and the left who took up E. P. Thompson's account of class and culture and later defended historical materialism against the linguistic turn. His first essay in Labour/Le Travailleur (1976) traced artisan culture and restated what he called 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history': 'As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop'; the critic David Bercuson read his study of Hamilton's skilled workers (1979) as 'echoing E.P. Thompson' (1981). In the International Labor and Working-Class History forum of 1987 he answered Joan Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which on his reading reduced class and its material relations to discourse, while granting, as Ted McCoy (2021) quotes him, that 'to say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters'; and Descent into Discourse (1990) held, as the Marxist reviewer Alex Callinicos quoted it, that 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected', while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'. Scott replied that 'class struggle is produced in discourse', a discourse she took to include 'ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies', not words alone, and that there is no choice, 'as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender'; Callinicos, broadly sympathetic, suggested that his treatment of class might underestimate 'the objective determinants of subjective action' and noted that he took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. In 2009 he criticised Ian McKay's liberal order as, in his reading, 'a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework' that 'sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Bryan D. Palmer (b. 1951); “Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective” (Labour/Le Travailleur, 1976); A Culture in Conflict: Skilled Workers and Industrial Capitalism in Hamilton, Ontario, 1860–1914 (1979); The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981); with Gregory S. Kealey, Dreaming of What Might Be: The Knights of Labor in Ontario, 1880–1900 (1982); Working-Class Experience (1983; 2nd ed. 1992); “Response to Joan Scott” (International Labor and Working-Class History, 1987); Descent into Discourse: The Reification of Language and the Writing of Social History (1990); “Homage to Edward Thompson” (Labour/Le Travail, 1993–94); E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994). After 2000: Canada’s 1960s (2009); “Radical Reasoning” (Underhill Review, 2009). Readings: Bercuson (1981); Scott’s reply (1987); Callinicos (1992); Dissenting Traditions (2021), with essays by Rogers, McCoy and Pearson.
nodes.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: his 1976 Labour/Le Travailleur essay in full; the first page of his 1987 'Response to Joan Scott' (publisher's preview image) and its notes as listed by the publisher; Scott's 1987 essay (first page) and her 'A Reply to Criticism' (1987) in full; Bercuson (1981, pp. 95–97); Callinicos's 1992 review of Descent into Discourse in full; 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993–94), searched in full and read at pp. 67–68 (Part I) and 16–18 (Part II); and 'Radical Reasoning' (2009) in full. Unread here: the monographs (A Culture in Conflict, Dreaming of What Might Be, Working-Class Experience), Descent into Discourse itself (borrow-only; its words are quoted as Callinicos quotes them, with his page references), pp. 15–23 of the 1987 response (quoted only through Scott's reply and through McCoy, 2021), The Making of E. P. Thompson (1981), Objections and Oppositions (1994) and Canada's 1960s (2009). He is not presented as a founder: Freeman (2002) names him with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay presents its thesis as 'a standard axiom of an emerging social history'. Contested in period by Bercuson (1981) on working-class culture, by Scott (1987) on language and gender, and, from a sympathetic Marxist position, by Callinicos (1992). The 2009 critique of the liberal order is dated in its label and text. The essays in Dissenting Traditions (2021) are later readings and are labelled as such wherever they are cited.

edges.relationship: Craft culture and class conflict: skilled workers' culture as a resource in working-class formation, from 'Most Uncommon Common Men' (1976) to A Culture in Conflict (1979), carried on with Kealey in Dreaming of What Might Be (1982; known here only through later readings); contested by Bercuson (1981)
edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statement. 'Most Uncommon Common Men: Craft and Culture in Historical Perspective', Labour/Le Travailleur 1 (1976), pp. 5–31, read in full in the journal's PDF. Artisan radicalism 'was part and parcel of a larger context, a matrix of institutions, ideologies and traditions which, taken together, define the contours of a singular culture' (p. 7); 'in viewing culture as a resource and society as the arena in which that resource is utilized, we are necessarily led to a refinement of our conception of the "levels" at which culture operates' (p. 8); 'It has become a standard axiom of an emerging social history of the working class that the artisan, not the debased proletarian, fathered the labour movement. As a class for itself, the working class was born, not in the factory, but in the workshop' (p. 14), where Thompson, the Webbs, Musson and Pelling are cited as agreeing on the skilled mechanic's influence. In-period reception, from a critic: David Bercuson, 'Through the Looking Glass of Culture', Labour/Le Travailleur 7 (1981), pp. 95–112, pp. 95–97 re-read in the journal's PDF. He quotes A Culture in Conflict (his n. 10: pp. xii–xiv) for a method of 'sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past', in which 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research', and (n. 11: p. xiii) for 'a tradition of empirical Marxism' (p. 96); 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (p. 97). Bercuson's methodological objection (pp. 107–108, read in the journal's PDF): 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; he asks whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107), and writes that 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108). Kealey's companion defence in the same issue defends class analysis and culture (wcreq_kealey_1981; not re-read in 1.134). A Culture in Conflict (1979), Dreaming of What Might Be (1982) and Working-Class Experience (1983; 1992) were not read here; they are cited at title level and through Bercuson. The edge's in-period evidence covers 1976–81; the 1982 Knights of Labor book is mentioned in the relationship text but rests only on McCoy's later quotation, so the label's dates stop at 1979. Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) reads A Culture in Conflict as following Thompson in finding resistance among skilled artisans and in quoting Thompson's working-class culture as a 'way of struggle' rather than a 'way of life' (citing pp. xii, xiv); Ted McCoy (2021) quotes Kealey and Palmer's chapter on the Knights: 'A subordinate class must reach toward an alternative hegemony if it ever hopes to dominate the ethos of society' (Dreaming, p. 277, as quoted). A contribution, not a founding: Freeman (2002) names Palmer with Kealey and Sangster in the founding generation of Labour/Le Travail, and the 1976 essay calls its thesis an axiom of an emerging field. edge_890 (ep_thompson → cdn_working_class) and edge_886 (marx → cdn_working_class) stay: they record the Thompsonian and Marxist resources and the 1981 debate; this edge records Palmer's own contribution.

edges.relationship: Answers Scott's case for reconceiving labour history through language and gender, which he read as reducing class and its material relations to discourse (International Labor and Working-Class History forum, 1987); Scott replied that class struggle is produced in discourse, which she defined to include institutions and social practices. Descent into Discourse (1990) was his subsequent book-length intervention
edges.evidence_note: Scott's position in her own words. 'On Language, Gender, and Working-Class History', International Labor and Working-Class History 31 (Spring 1987), pp. 1–13; only p. 1 was read (publisher's preview image): gender 'has not been considered seriously for what it could provide in the way of a major reconceptualization of (labor) history'; theories of language 'offer a way of thinking about how people construct meaning, about how difference (and therefore sexual difference) operates in the construction of meaning'; labour historians' recent articles on 'language' 'reduce this important concept to the study of "words"' (p. 1). Palmer's response in the same issue, 'Response to Joan Scott', pp. 14–23; only p. 14 (preview image) and the notes listed by the publisher were read. It opens on the Halifax strikes of August 1842, with Palmer imagining himself at the scene, 'Conscious of "the need to avoid economic determinism" and aware of the extent to which "our needs are made of words"', thirsting 'for a dialogue with the participants that will both reveal all and deepen the discourse' (p. 14); n. 2 says the quoted phrases come from Stedman Jones's introduction to Languages of Class and from Ignatieff, 'texts that I take to be related to one another'. Scott's 'A Reply to Criticism', ILWCH 32 (Fall 1987), pp. 39–45, read in full, reports and quotes his response: Palmer and Christine Stansell 'share a fundamental disagreement with my emphasis on "language," arguing instead that material reality, social experiences, real or concrete events are the stuff of social history' (p. 39); she quotes his 'No discourse today! The class struggle has intervened' and answers: 'The opposition discourse versus class struggle is one I cannot accept, for class struggle is produced in discourse'; 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 40). She defines the term at once: 'By discourse I do not mean utterances, or "words" ... but whole ways of thinking, of understanding how the world operates and what one's place is in it. And not only ways of thinking, but ways of organizing lives, institutions, societies, ways of implementing and justifying inequalities, but also of refusing them'; to say that 'the working class family was created within working-class discourse' 'is not to say that "words" alone brought families into being' (p. 40). The reduction-to-discourse objection is therefore Palmer's interpretation of her argument, which she rejected. She says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me, and little of it has to do with either women or gender' (p. 41), that he implies she has deviated from Marx's dialectical and historical materialism, to which she answers that 'there is more to Marx, greater complexity in his materialism, than Palmer's crude invocation of it' (p. 43), and that 'There is no choice, as Bryan Palmer insists there is, between a focus on class or gender; each is necessarily incomplete without the other' (p. 45). These are Scott's characterisations of his text. The forum had four voices, not two camps. Christine Stansell ('A Response to Joan Scott', pp. 24–29; only p. 24 read, publisher's preview image) called Scott's essay 'a welcome and important attempt to import some of the sophisticated concerns of current literary criticism into labor history' and sided 'with Joan Scott in believing that historians' willful lack of interest in poststructuralist debate is our loss—or, more properly, our missed opportunity' (p. 24). Anson Rabinbach ('Rationalism and Utopia as Languages of Nature: A Note', pp. 30–36; only p. 30 read) restated with approval her case that Stedman Jones's language 'is as instrumentalized in the notion of politics as economic interest is in the notion of class' (p. 30). Scott grouped Palmer with Stansell on 'language' and wrote that Rabinbach 'endorses and expands on my analysis' (p. 39); she answered Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (p. 42) and Rabinbach's case for rationalism and universalism (p. 44) separately. The rest of Stansell's and Rabinbach's essays was not read. Later readings, labelled as such: Ted McCoy (2021) quotes the response: 'To say that language matters is not to say it is all that matters' (p. 16, emphasis original) and 'Class is indeed a difficult development to grasp precisely because in both its subjective and objective guises it reproduces the social order at the same time as it challenges it. Language and gender figure in this decisively' (p. 22); he reads Palmer as granting that attention to the gendered features of language is 'indisputable'. Descent into Discourse (1990; unread here) carried the dispute into its chapter on gender: Nicholas Rogers (2021) and Chad Pearson (2021) quote it on Scott's appraisal of women in The Making of the English Working Class: in Pearson's quotation it 'thus tilts too problematically toward the determining power of discourse' (p. 85), while Rogers paraphrases it as tilting 'too problematically towards' it, and as quoting Scott's 'There is no social experience apart from people's perception of it' (p. 180), the sentence read above in her 1987 reply. The arrow records Palmer's critique and Scott's rejoinder; it does not judge the dispute. Scott's own critique of Thompson's gendered account of class remains on edge_314 (gender → ep_thompson).

edges.relationship: Descent into Discourse: the linguistic turn in social history criticised as a 'reification of language', with class held to originate in relations of production rather than in discourse; Stedman Jones's languages of class a principal target (1987–90)
edges.evidence_note: The book (Temple University Press, 1990) was not read: the Internet Archive copies are borrow-only and its search-inside service returned HTTP 403. Its wording is taken from an in-period review that quotes it with page numbers: Alex Callinicos, Labour/Le Travail 29 (1992), pp. 311–313, read in full in the journal's PDF. Callinicos quotes Palmer: 'Much writing that appears under the designer label of poststructuralism/post modernism is, quite bluntly, crap' (199); Callinicos describes Palmer's standpoint, in his own words, as 'not that of a defensive empiricism but of a critical, anti-Stalinist Marxism', and quotes the book: 'historical materialism remains the foundation upon which studies of the past must be erected' (xiii); yet discourse theory 'contains insights and guides capable of opening new doors of understanding to historians committed to a materialism that recognizes the need for a rigorous reading of documents and texts/contexts' (189). The book is 'a critical survey of "the reification of language"' from the Russian Formalists through Foucault and Derrida that 'traces the vulgarization of their ideas by historians working in the fields of politics, gender, and class' (p. 312). Against 'the reduction by Gareth Stedman Jones et al. of class as a discursive construct', Palmer writes that 'class relations are, in origin, economic relations rooted in the capitalist process of accumulation, whereby one social stratum expropriates surplus from another' (138) (p. 312). Callinicos's in-period objections: Palmer is 'too willing to fall in line with the dominant way in which poststructuralism has been received in the English-speaking world' and misreads Foucault's Archaeology (p. 312); his claim that 'class as an objective economic reality is not present before the arrival of industrial capitalism' (139) sits oddly with Ste Croix; 'Perhaps, like Edward Thompson before him, Palmer has reacted to the dissolution of agency into structure by underestimating the objective determinants of subjective action' (p. 313). He calls the results 'admirable' and his disagreements 'relatively minor' (p. 312). The target was already set in 1987: Palmer's ILWCH response (p. 14 and n. 2, read) borrows phrases from Stedman Jones's Languages of Class for the first-person scene that opens it, and Scott's reply says 'Most of his critique is directed at Stedman Jones, not me' (ILWCH 32, p. 41). Later readings, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer in 1993 granting that 'Poststructurally inclined historians rightly stress the need for closer attention to language and representation' ('The Poverty of Theory Revisited', Left History 1:1, 1993, p. 94, as quoted; unread here); Finkel (2021) calls the book Palmer's 'anger with the discursive turn'. Scope: a critique of the linguistic turn's treatment of class, not of attention to language as such. edge_105 (language → social) and edge_200 (historyworkshop–language) stay.

edges.relationship: Liberal order criticised as an elastic, seemingly trans-historical category that sidesteps capitalism's changing historical structures, in a review of McKay's Reasoning Otherwise (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. 'Radical Reasoning', a feature review essay on Ian McKay, Reasoning Otherwise (2008), The Underhill Review (Carleton University), Fall 2009, read in full (web text; locators below are pages of the print PDF, https://www3.carleton.ca/underhillreview/09/fall/reviews/print/Palmer.pdf). He reads McKay's liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism', and says past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order."' 'As an elastic category, liberal order can contain almost anything associated with what has traditionally been understood about modern developing societies'. 'The danger in deploying liberal order in this way, as a seemingly trans-historical analytic framework, is that it actually sidesteps the need to confront and elucidate capitalism's changing historical structures'; 'it may well be impossible to discern anything distinctly Canadian about the notion of liberal order'; 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression.' He adds that McKay's 'elastic understanding of Gramsci's hegemony conflates what Gramsci differentiated as a "separation of powers"'. The elasticity and capitalism argument is at pp. 3–4 and the Gramsci criticism at pp. 4–5. Qualifications kept: 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself' (p. 4), and the book 'stands as an undeniable achievement' (p. 31). This is Palmer's interpretation of the framework. McKay's own position, recorded under lof_mckay_2009 and known here through Fecteau's quotation, distinguishes the two analytically while treating them as historically close: 'Liberal order and capitalism cannot be conflated. Yet, after the 1840s, they also could not be easily separated' (p. 385, as quoted by Fecteau, 2009). That chapter appeared in the same year and is not a reply to Palmer; no direct rejoinder was found. Scope: the essay reviews Reasoning Otherwise and quotes Rebels, Reds, Radicals (2005, p. 84); it does not discuss the 2000 prospectus directly. McKay's reply, if any, was not checked. The critique-audit of 2026-10-14 proposed a group edge cdn_working_class → liberal_order_framework on this text; with the person entry, the person edge carries it and the group edge is not proposed. edge_845 (karl–liberal_order_framework, comparison) stays.

edges.relationship: Thompson's history of class and culture as a model for Palmer's labour history and the subject of his studies of Thompson (1976–94), with disagreements Palmer stated, including on base and superstructure
edges.evidence_note: In-period evidence. Palmer's 1976 essay (read) cites Thompson's Making for the skilled mechanic's leading role (p. 14 and notes). Bercuson (1981, p. 97, re-read): 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes."' Kealey (1981, p. 82; existing note, not re-read) cites Palmer's forthcoming book as the place where Thompson's work is analysed at length. Palmer's 1987 ILWCH response (notes as listed by the publisher) leans on Thompson: n. 8 cites The Making (pp. 529–40) for how historians have interrogated the language of sources, n. 10 says 'This unity of the political and the economic is fundamental to Thompson's Making', and n. 14 cites The Poverty of Theory (pp. 235–36). 'Homage to Edward Thompson', Labour/Le Travail 32 (1993) and 33 (1994), read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18: Palmer sets out Thompson's socialist humanism against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor' (Part I, p. 68) and quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (Part II, p. 17; Thompson's interviews, cited in n. 9, not read). Palmer's two books on Thompson, The Making of E. P. Thompson: Marxism, Humanism, and History (1981) and E. P. Thompson: Objections and Oppositions (1994), are cited at title and imprint level only (Open Library). Stated disagreement, in period: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) notes that Descent into Discourse 'takes Thompson and Raymond Williams to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure' (pp. 209–11 of the book, unread here). Later readings, labelled as such: Nicholas Rogers (2021) quotes Palmer's 1993 interview in Left History: 'it was relooking at The Making that convinced me to do labour history' (Left History 1:2, 1993, pp. 111–12, as quoted; the journal's PDF was behind a bot wall); Rogers calls The Making 'an exemplary model' for Palmer's dissertation, finds Palmer 'sympathetic and defensive of Thompson's position', but notes that 'Palmer does not necessarily agree with Thompson's reading of Marx' and 'is not a wholehearted advocate of Thompson's socialist humanism', since he holds to a revolutionary vanguard. Influence, not discipleship: the arrow records Thompson's work as Palmer's model and subject; it does not claim that Palmer adopted Thompson's positions whole.

edges.relationship: From within Marxism, rejects the 'economic automatism' of Stalinist base-and-superstructure Marxism and the treatment of class as 'a thing', holding to the 'dialectical interaction between social consciousness ... and social being' and faulting Marx's own 'clumsy static model' (1957–78)
edges.evidence_note: Thompson's own in-period statements. (1) 'Socialist Humanism: An Epistle to the Philistines', The New Reasoner 1 (Summer 1957), pp. 105–143, read in full in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription (no page numbers). Of Stalinist theory: 'How much easier if the people had no minds, if the "superstructure" was cut out and society was all "base"'; 'This economic automatism certainly is not Marxism.' 'In all their historical analysis Marx and Engels always kept in view this dialectical interaction between social consciousness (both active and passive) and social being. But in trying to explain their ideas they expressed them as a make-belief "model", the "basis" of social relations (in production) and the "superstructure" ... In fact no such basis and superstructure ever existed; it is a metaphor to help us to understand what does exist – men, who act, experience, think and act again. It turns out that it is a bad and dangerous model, since Stalin used it not as an image of men changing in society but as a mechanical model, operating semi-automatically and independently of conscious human agency.' 'An idea is not a reflex of a gasometer'; 'No "basis" ever invented a steam engine, or sat on the National Coal Board.' He does not exempt Marx: 'because Marx reduced his concept of process to a clumsy static model, Stalinism evolved this mystique'; features of Stalinism 'can be traced to ambiguities in the thought of Marx and, even more, to mechanistic fallacies in Lenin's writings'. Stalinism's three features are 'anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'. The revolt against Stalinism 'will, if successful, confirm the revolutionary confidence of the founders of the socialist movement'. (2) Preface to The Making of the English Working Class (1963), university-hosted transcription read in full (transcription pp. 1–2; printed pagination not collated): class is 'something which in fact happens (and can be shown to have happened) in human relationships'; 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing', in which the class-consciousness that '"it" ought to have' is deduced and 'a cultural superstructure' lets recognition dawn 'in inefficient ways'; 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' The same passage finds 'a similar error ... on the other side of the ideological divide', in the static sociology of Smelser and Dahrendorf, so the preface's target is reification in both camps. The preface's 'I am seeking to rescue the poor stockinger ...' is aimed at Fabian, economic-historian and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies, not at Marxism, and is not used here. (3) 'The Poverty of Theory' (1978), section x, re-read in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription: 'Stalinism afforded a caricature of Marxism, which offered ... an identical reification of process, in which a "superstructure" was reduced to confirming or legitimating a base' (the identity is with Smelser's sociology), and no analogies 'derived from mechanical or organic mechanism' can 'encompass the logic of indeterminate historical process', since no analogy from another area can have 'any more than a limited, illustrative, metaphoric value (and often, as with basis and superstructure, a static and damaging one)'; in section vii he calls himself 'deeply indebted for certain concepts to Marx's own practice'. In-period readings: Palmer's 'Homage to Edward Thompson' (1993, Part I, p. 68) describes Thompson's socialist humanism as directed against 'the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor', and (1994, Part II, p. 17) quotes Thompson calling The Making 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' (from interviews, not read). The critique was itself contested inside Marxism: Callinicos (1992, p. 313) reports that Palmer's Descent into Discourse took Thompson and Raymond Williams 'to task for abandoning the metaphor of base and superstructure'. Later reading, labelled as such: Rogers (2021) sees in Thompson a 'rejection of economic determinism and the base–superstructure model of explanation favoured by many Marxists', preferring 'the co-determination of social being and social consciousness, mediated by experience'. Scope: a critique of economistic and Stalinist uses of historical materialism, and of Marx's own static model, made from within Marxism; it is not a rejection of historical materialism. The Althusser critique stays on edge_310 (ep_thompson → althusser) and edge_027 (marx → althusser); his contribution to Marxist social history stays on edge_309 (ep_thompson → marx).

verification.note: Read in full in the Marxists Internet Archive transcription (from a PDF on the Barry Amiel & Norman Melburn Trust site; transcribed by Einde O'Callaghan); the transcription gives the issue and pp. 105–143 but no page breaks, and was not collated with the print. Palmer's Homage (1993) gives the same citation (New Reasoner 1, Summer 1957, 105–43). Passages used: 'if the "superstructure" was cut out and society was all "base"'; 'This economic automatism certainly is not Marxism'; the 'dialectical interaction between social consciousness (both active and passive) and social being'; basis and superstructure 'a metaphor' and 'a bad and dangerous model'; 'An idea is not a reflex of a gasometer'; 'No "basis" ever invented a steam engine'; Marx's 'clumsy static model'; 'ambiguities in the thought of Marx and, even more, to mechanistic fallacies in Lenin's writings'; 'anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'; the revolt 'will, if successful, confirm the revolutionary confidence of the founders of the socialist movement'.

sources.scope_note: Thompson's 1957 critique of Stalinist base-and-superstructure Marxism, from within the socialist tradition.

wcreq_bercuson_1981.note: Pp. 95–97 and 107–108 re-read for the 1.134 person entry in the PDF on the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/2658). p. 96: the new labour history's method 'as Palmer describes it' ('sharp detail of limited chronology or restricted region to illustrate the human dimensions of the past'; 'theory is meant to inform historical inquiry and, in turn, to be informed by historical research'; n. 10: A Culture in Conflict, xii–xiv) and 'what Palmer labels "a tradition of empirical Marxism"' (n. 11: xiii). p. 97: 'Palmer calls the skilled the cutting edge of the working class. They could just as easily be labelled the rearguard'; 'Palmer, echoing E.P. Thompson, regards culture and conflict as "complementary processes"' (n. 13: xii). pp. 107–108: 'Historians must prove that Canadian workers, men and women, skilled and unskilled, were bound by a common culture that was primarily the product of their class experience before they can use culture to explain anything'; workers 'seem to have responded as much from consciousness of job, place, church, ethnic group, and other factors as from a culture of class'; whether 'class was a more important means of self-identification than gender' (p. 107); 'Even if Thompson is right about England, his concepts do not necessarily apply anywhere else' (p. 108).

lof_palmer_2009.note: Re-read in full for the 1.134 person entry (Carleton Underhill Review page, Fall 2009, 'Feature Review Essay'; unpaginated). Added to the earlier note: liberal order as a project 'in which liberty, equality, and private property are sanctified as the foundations of a civil society that valorizes individualism'; past leftists 'never spoke of an enemy that they named "liberal order"'; the full sentence 'The most serious problem with the liberal order perspective, then, is that it allows mainstream historians to avoid confronting just how critically important it is to name the frontline enemy: capitalism as systematic exploitation and endlessly proliferating oppression'; the qualification 'McKay is not necessarily captive of such tendencies himself'; Reasoning Otherwise 'stands as an undeniable achievement'.

pl129_palmer_1993_homage.note: Both parts downloaded from the journal's site (https://lltjournal.ca/index.php/llt/article/view/4897 and /4917) for the 1.134 drafts, searched in full and read at Part I pp. 67–68 and Part II pp. 16–18. Part I, p. 68: Thompson's socialist humanism against Stalinism, 'governed as it was by anti-intellectualism, moral nihilism, and the denial of the creative agency of human labour'; 'In the mechanical idealism of Stalinism's appropriation of the base/superstructure metaphor, all of humanity's being could be reduced to a mere reflection of the economic substance of society'; n. 64 cites 'Socialist Humanism' and 'Agency and Choice' and Palmer's own Making of E.P. Thompson, 48–51. Part II, p. 17: The Making as 'a polemic against abbreviated economistic notations of Marxism' in which 'the creation of the working class was that of a determined process: steam power plus the factory system equals the working class', quoting Thompson from interviews (n. 9 lists Hogben 1988, Scott 1980 and the Visions of History interview; not read). Part II, p. 18: 'the historian has got to be listening all the time'. A Thompson admirer's in-period reading (1993–94), not Thompson's own text.

thompson_making_preface.note: Re-read in full for the 1.134 extra edge (ep_thompson → karl). Transcription pp. 1–2: 'There is today an ever-present temptation to suppose that class is a thing. This was not Marx's meaning, in his own historical writing, yet the error vitiates much latter-day "Marxist" writing'; the class-consciousness '"it" ought to have'; 'a cultural superstructure, through which this recognition dawns in inefficient ways'; 'a similar error is committed daily on the other side of the ideological divide' (Smelser, Dahrendorf); 'If we remember that class is a relationship and not a thing, we can not think in this way.' Transcription p. 3: the 'enormous condescension of posterity' passage answers Fabian, empirical economic-history and 'Pilgrim's Progress' orthodoxies. Rogers (2021, n. 1) places the class-consciousness passage at pp. 9–10 of the 1968 Penguin edition; printed pages were not checked.

ep_thompson_poverty.note: Sections vii and x re-read for the 1.134 extra edge. Section x: 'Stalinism afforded a caricature of Marxism, which offered, in very different terminology but with an equally abstracted vocabulary, an identical reification of process, in which a "superstructure" was reduced to confirming or legitimating a base' (the comparison is with Smelser), followed by Stalin's 1950 formulations; no analogy from another area can have 'any more than a limited, illustrative, metaphoric value (and often, as with basis and superstructure, a static and damaging one)'. Section vii: 'Insofar as I am myself deeply indebted for certain concepts to Marx's own practice, I refuse to evade responsibility by falling back upon his authority'. Transcription without print pagination.

rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13). Palmer's work is read across Canadian working-class history, the linguistic-turn debate, the liberal order debate and the history of the 1960s; he already holds roster rows in cdn_working_class, cdn_sixties, liberal_order_framework and who_killed_debate. In-period evidence: his own 1976 essay (read in full) and the first page and notes of his 1987 response to Scott; Scott's 1987 essay (first page) and her reply (in full); Bercuson's 1981 critique; Callinicos's 1992 review of Descent into Discourse, which quotes the book with page numbers; Palmer's 1993–94 'Homage to Edward Thompson'; and the 2009 Underhill Review essay. Nicholas Rogers's chapter in Dissenting Traditions (AU Press, 2021) and the chapters by McCoy and Pearson are labelled later readings. The Thompson edge rests on 'Socialist Humanism' (1957), the Making preface (1963) and The Poverty of Theory (1978), all read in transcription. Dissertation evidence, metadata only and never in entry text: 125 Canadian History PhDs (2009–2026) cite Palmer, with readership dispersion 0.79 across 5 co-citation fields; most of those citations are to Canada's 1960s and the 1992 synthesis. This measures Canadian reading, not his importance (user).

row.context: Criticised the linguistic turn in social history as a 'reification of language' (Descent into Discourse, 1990, as quoted by Callinicos, 1992), while granting that discourse theory 'contains insights and guides'; Scott answered him in 1987 that class struggle is produced in discourse.
